body.head: GOOD-BYE MY FANCY: THE STRUGGLE AND LABOR OF LATE LIFE

div.p: Despite the press signaling that “it seems probable that [November Boughs] will be the last published by Walt Whitman,”—a fair prognostication, since the book’s release came just a few months after another paralytic stroke—Whitman continued writing and contributing pieces to newspapers and magazines for the next three years. As early as March 1890, Whitman’s letters refer to “another annex” (loc.07729), which he envisions in July as twelve pages of poetry (loc.07796). In a letter to Richard Maurice Bucke on November 12, he declares that he “Shall call my little 2d annex ‘Good Bye My Fancy’ after a little piece in it” (loc.07856). “There was a rotundness to Whitman’s last year,” suggests biographer David S. Reynolds, “a sense that he was saying what he had to say and finishing what he had to finish” (585). Even in rapidly declining health, Whitman continued to envision cultural contributions in the form of his “annexes,” a word he favored with an etymology denoting “to tie together” and “to connect and fasten.” Late life gave Whitman the opportunity to tie up artistic loose ends, to bring together the highlights of his lifework, and to fasten them between covers with an eye to future generations of readers.

Though he might have been planning the work as early as March 1890, it was around late November that Whitman began compiling the manuscript of what he would call his “old age collation.” The November 29 issue of the Critic carried a note written by the poet himself announcing that “Walt Whitman is putting the later touches to a volume called ‘Good-Bye My Fancy,’ containing his old age songlets, and intended as a ‘second annex and completion’ to Leaves of Grass” (“Of Making Many Books” 18).The announcement was reprinted in the December 12, 1890, issue of The Philadelphia Inquirer under the heading “Walt Whitman is Doing,” which Traubel records in WWC 7:352. For the manuscript of this announcement, see WWA ID: uva.00395. According to Whitman’s preface to the volume, Good-Bye My Fancy was written to “while away the hours of my 72nd year—hours of forced confinement in my den.” Horace Traubel extensively documents Whitman’s process. On December 9, Traubel asks how work on the second annex is progressing, to which Whitman responds that he is “pegging away at it the best I can” (WWC 7:342). Later, Traubel offers a glimpse into this “pegging” process:
7:20 P.M. W. in his own room—had untied manuscript “Good-Bye My Fancy”—had it spread out in his lap, the table, the bed. Arranging—as, he said, he would probably arrange a dozen times more before he was satisfied. Some of the copy in print, some in manuscript. Had spent one of his “usual days”—with, perhaps, more ease than before. (December 17, 1890; 7:360)
The manuscript referred to here is likely one now housed in the Charles E. Feinberg Collection at the Library of Congress, comprised of seventy-eight numbered pages with proof sheets, newspaper clippings, and original holographs pasted on the versos of large yellow papers (loc.05454). Having the text on only one side of the paper would have allowed the partially paralyzed Whitman to scan the contents more easily; he could spread out the manuscript around his chair, removing the necessity to turn pages.

When Daniel Brinton asked about the book’s progress, Whitman replied, “It is hardly to be dignified as ‘work’: it is simply a last drop, a leavetaking, my farewell—a gout” (WWC 8:58).Whitman’s prefatory note for Brinton’s book, Giordano Bruno: Philosopher and Martyr, is included in Good-Bye My Fancy. Whitman played around with this “last drop” imagery for his second annex, shown in a manuscript reproduced by Traubel which includes a great variation in possible titles, including “Farewell Drops of a Passing Shower,” “Departing Drops of a Passing Rain,” “Belated Drops of a Passing Shower,” and “Last Drops of a Passing Shower” (WWC 8:308; fig. 1). By November 1890, he had settled on Good-Bye My Fancy, just one possible title among many scrawled around “2d Annex” in the manuscript. “I know ‘Fancy’ has come to express a more or less circumscribed idea,” Whitman told Traubel, “that imagination covers larger areas—is the new statement” (WWC 8:43). Whitman is perhaps referring to the more psychological uses of the term that became prominent by the late nineteenth century, in which “fancy” was synonymous with the hallucinatory—the fantastic. “Yet,” he adds, “‘Fancy’ has generic warrant—[I’m] using it because I am confident readers will so comprehend it.” This is to say, within the genre constraints of poetry, “Fancy” carries more weight than “imagination”—a more recent addition to the lexicon—so readers of poetry will find the title more self-consciously poetic. As Harold Aspiz proposes in his close reading of one of the volume’s eponymous poems, the embodied fancy is “the shaping spirit of his imagination” (236). For Robert Creeley, fancy is “where thought and sense find a way of meeting” (65). The word as a noun is notably absent from previous editions of Leaves of Grass, where its closest analog is Whitman’s expansive self, the all-embracing persona. Thus, as he approached old age, the Whitmanic self became more etherealized—less dependent on weighty matter; the self has become the fancy. Another draft of the miscellany’s cover page suggests that Good-Bye My Fancy is a collection “to taper off Leaves of Grass” (quoted WWC 8:335, manuscript in the Feinberg Collection of the Library of Congress). Whitman here envisions these poems not as a “conclusion” to Leaves of Grass, but a gradual diminishing of his carefully curated voice, a final phase in the waning of his poetic project.

The draft of a title page given in With Walt Whitman in Camden titles the book “Good-Bye My Fancy / and Other Songlets. . .,” suggesting that “Good-Bye My Fancy” is one “songlet” among others. There is a sort of nesting-doll structure in the finished book: “Good-Bye My Fancy” is the title of two poems in a cluster of thirty-one called “Good-Bye My Fancy” in the book called Good-Bye My Fancy. Whitman seems to have toyed with several iterations of an old-age cluster before arriving at the one found in the volume. In one cluster, titled “An Old Man’s Recitatives” (loc.00230), Whitman pastes together proof sheets of “Old Chants” (here retitled “Ancient Songs Reciting”), “Grand is the Seen,” “Death Dogs my Steps” (a three-line poem that becomes the conclusion of the longer “L. of G.’s Purport”), and “For us Two, Dear Reader.” All of these pieces appear later in Good-Bye My Fancy, though not in that order. Read as a cluster, the four poems dramatically enact the ebbing away of voice, with each growing progressively shorter from the twenty-five-line “Ancient Songs Reciting” to the final two-line “For us Two, Dear Reader.” According to Whitman’s hand annotation on this manuscript, he had sent the cluster to Scribner’s Magazine on December 17, 1890, and received a notice of rejection about a month later. Whitman tried using this four-poem structure with diminishing line counts again in “Old Age Echoes,” which he sent to Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine—also in December.According to Whitman’s daybooks, a cluster called “Old Age’s Echoes” was sent to Harper’s New Monthly Magazine on October 18, 1889, and later rejected by editor Henry M. Alden (DBN 535). The same cluster, which he described as “3 or 4 sonato poemets,” was later rejected by Nineteenth Century magazine after Whitman submitted it in November (DBN 539-540). Here, “Sounds of the Winter,” “The Unexpress’d,” “Sail Out for Good, Eidólon Yacht”—three poems of seven, ten, and nine lines respectively—culminate in another two-line poem, “After the Argument.” Whitman originally intended “To the Sunset Breeze” to be the cluster’s third poem, but it was replaced when the cluster appeared in Lippincott’s March 1891 issue. For some reason, both short concluding poems in these clusters do not get placed in “Good-Bye My Fancy” beside their lengthier partners, but instead become the two concluding poems of “Some Laggards Yet,” an odd assemblage of poetry and prose more than midway through the volume.

With these two old-age clusters in the mail to prospective periodicals, December 1890 was a busy month for the poet, who worked daily on composing and arranging his creative output. Clusters and individual poems were going out, even while the manuscript of Good-Bye My Fancy was developing. Traubel’s entry for December 17 ties Whitman’s editing of the miscellany to his health, noting that the poet had spent “one of his ‘usual days,’” though he perhaps felt “more ease.” We get a sense of Whitman’s “usual days” by examining his letters to Bucke throughout the month. On December 3, Bucke mentioned to Whitman that Traubel had given “a very good account of your condition—says you look and seem better and are a little more cheerful” (loc.07131). This was just one day before Whitman wrote to Bucke about feeling “mainly the same—poorly” (loc.08260). Significantly, this was the month in which Whitman had a urine test confirming that, while his kidneys were in working order, he suffered from an enlarged prostate, causing intense discomfort; Bucke recommended catheterization, saying, “your main difficulty is that on account of the enlargement of the prostate the bladder is not entirely emptied at any time—the urine retained undergoes decomposition and causes irritation” (loc.07135). The poet complained of “head uncomfortable & aching,” a “suspicion of belly ache,” indigestion and “slow & hard & sluggish” bowel movements (loc.07858;loc.07859). On the twelfth, Whitman again noted stomach pain, strongest in the morning but subsiding by the evening. The same letter also records an outing in his wheelchair on the next day, and his “mark’d symptoms of cold in the head” (loc.07860). Later that evening, Whitman felt “neglected here badly” and “probably chill’d” from his excursion. On December 14, Whitman had a successful bowel movement but expressed concern that he had caught a chill the day before—a fear worsened by reports of Asiatic flu in the area (loc.08093). Two days later, his bowel movements were “so-so,” though he felt “sluggish quite always but not at all as bad as a year & a half ago” (loc.07862). By then end of the month, however, he was feeling “tolerably easy,” with good bowel movements, and was again enjoying outings in his wheelchair (loc.07861).

In January 1891, Traubel again depicts Whitman laying out the Good-Bye My Fancy manuscript around his chair and having some indecision in ordering its contents (WWC 7:413). Throughout March and April, Whitman’s letters mention reading the proofs from David McKay (loc.07905;loc.08032). Finally, the copyright was secured on May 18. George Sloan Ferguson, the Irish-born printer whose firm set the type for November Boughs, finished the printing later that month, and Frederick Oldach was quick with the binding—both companies working far quicker than they had on November Boughs. This was thanks to quick proofing by Whitman, who raced through the book’s production despite chronic depression (see DBN 2:587). On April 13, Traubel records Whitman’s “mental depression,” echoing an entry on March 15 of Whitman’s suffering from “the great depression,” which again echoes a similar entry on February 7 (WWC 8:144; 8:78; 7:452). By late April, Whitman confided to Dr. John Johnston that he was suffering from the “worst kind” of depression. In mid-May, he wrote of “pretty bad times with me—low ebb” to Bucke (loc.08036;loc08047). Jerome Loving has rightly summarized Good-Bye My Fancy as Whitman “packing his literary bags for eternity…[anticipating] his own impending death.” However, one wonders about the inner-conflict in the depressed, ailing poet reading proof sheets written in a tone Loving describes as one of “wonderment instead of fear” (476). Could the work of compiling this miscellany—laying out the annotated proof sheets around his upstairs confinement—have been a sort of therapy for Whitman? Also therapeutic could have been the thought of another last cultural contribution—a final mark on the literary world.

div.head: Whitman’s Physical and Mental Health
div.p: Biographers and scholars identify periods of depression in Whitman’s life; 1858 and the early 1870s have been identified as especially bad. Despite Whitman’s history of depression, Traubel often disagrees with the poet’s self-assessment in 1890. For example, on April 29, shortly before the publication of Good-Bye My Fancy: “W. seemed to me better—whether because he had just finished his meal I do not know—since he said, ‘I am not better—I have suffered another of the very meanest days.’ But while he looked pale and worn, voice and manner were certainly fuller and more vigorous” (WWC 8:170). Traubel’s eagerness to contend with Whitman’s self-diagnosis may have been wishful thinking, a willingness to overlook the triggers of geriatric depression and its manifestations. It is certainly no coincidence that Whitman began frequently referring to his depressed mental state around the time of death of his favorite brother, Thomas Jefferson Whitman, in November 1890. “Some bereaved persons experience unyielding, extreme preoccupation and longing for their lost loved one,” suggests Gary J. Kennedy, Director of the Division of Geriatric Psychiatry at Montefiore Medical Center (25). “They seem unable to stop grieving,” he concludes. The period surrounding the compiling, proofing, and publishing of Good-Bye My Fancy was, for Whitman, one marked by depression, made particularly acute by the loss of Jeff.

Of course, Whitman had faced tragic losses before, including both his mother and his sister-in-law Mattie in 1873, the same year he had another stroke. In the autobiographical sketch included in Good-Bye My Fancy, Whitman writes that 1873 was “lost,” due to the deaths of “the two best and sweetest women I have ever seen or known” and his stroke, “the result of too extreme bodily and mental strain” from his service during the war. While the frequency of losses in age can put one into perpetual mourning, especially when one loses a favorite sibling, Jeff’s death might have exacerbated the poet’s chronic depression in late 1890 chiefly in its confluence with other personal struggles. “Although loss of friends and family is an inevitable consequence of aging,” Gary J. Kennedy argues, “it is declining health and the onset of disability that are the twin determinants of the majority of depressive symptoms and disorders in late life” (2). Elsewhere Kennedy suggests that depressed senescent patients often suffer “grief for the loss of the healthy self” (85). Whitman’s frequent allusions to his paralysis, dimming eyesight, and invalidism in Good-Bye My Fancy and his extensive correspondence from the period perform a grieving for the healthy self so celebrated in his earlier writings. “I doubt if a heartier, stronger, healthier physique, more balanced upon itself, or more unconscious, more sound, ever lived, from 1835 to ‘72,” his autobiographical sketch continues. This almost superhuman past self is implicitly idolized in contrast with his current condition: “Bodily I am completely disabled. . . .”

Good-Bye My Fancy’s inclusion of the previously unpublished “Health, Old Style” is another noteworthy example of Whitman grieving his lost state (42–43). He appends a short prose note to “Health,” a rhymed and metered poem—twelve stanzas in iambic pentameter and ballad form—purportedly “found originally in some scrap-book fifty years ago.” The poem, which Whitman calls “a favorite of mine,” was written by English dramatist and poet George Davies Harley, and first appeared in the June 1797 issue of The Monthly Mirror. The inclusion of a poem by another author turns Good-Bye My Fancy, already a miscellany, into a scrapbook in its own right. The poem appears in its entirety, adding over a full page of text to an otherwise small volume, and pads out the page count with a celebration of “ruddy health in rude majestic state” and “sinewy functions.” The manuscript of “Health, Old Style” in the Library of Congress is a stained and tattered copy of the poem pasted onto the large yellow sheets of paper on which Whitman was organizing the contents of Good-Bye My Fancy. Whitman calls the poem a “glaring contrast to my present bodily state,” alluding to those lines praising one “from pain, from sorrow free, / The lengthen’d life with peerless joy replete.” As the examination of Whitman’s correspondence from 1890 and 1891 demonstrates, his late life was one of virtually unrelenting physical pain and depression. Though there certainly were some bright moments, his final years were not marked by “peerless joy,” however refreshing he found the occasional evening breeze.

div.head: David McKay, “Whitman’s most successful publisher”
div.p: Creating Whitman’s final books depended on his network of trusted compositors, proofers, and binders. Whitman’s publisher, David McKay, played a crucial role in this network. The publishing of Whitman’s final miscellany, and its incorporation into the deathbed edition of Leaves of Grass in 1892, brought his relationship with McKay full circle; their relationship began with the publisher’s willingness in 1882 to issue the infamously “banned in Boston” sixth edition of Leaves of Grass, which was originally published by James R. Osgood (See Folsom, Whitman Making Books 47-54). At the time, McKay was only twenty-one and working for the Philadelphia printer Rees Welsh, described by historian Charles Green as “primarily a used book distributor and small publisher of law books . . . interested in expanding its offerings” (127). Perhaps it was McKay’s youthful outlook that allowed him to see what Osgood had neglected: that no publicity is bad publicity, and offering a “banned” book can be decidedly good for business. He took a chance that paid off, with the book quickly going through five printings in 1882 alone. Within the year, McKay bought out Rees Welsh and issued Leaves of Grass and Specimen Days & Collect with his own name proudly on the title pages. He did all this within ten years of immigrating to the United States from his native Scotland.

For the next decade, McKay not only published books by Whitman, but also books from Whitman’s main apologists, creating a sort of “Whitman canon,” a network of literature by and about the poet. These included Richard Maurice Bucke’s biography, Walt Whitman (1883), Elizabeth Porter Gould’s Gems from Walt Whitman (1889), William Sloane Kennedy’s The Poet as a Craftsman (1886), and Traubel’s Camden’s Compliment to Walt Whitman (1889). Within this time, Leaves of Grass went through twelve printings, and was joined by Specimen Days, November Boughs, Complete Poems & Prose, and Good-Bye My Fancy. Looking back at his work with Whitman, McKay called those ten years “never-to-be-forgotten days.” While celebrating himself as “Whitman’s most successful publisher,” McKay recognized that the poet was more than just another client: “No one could enter the charmed circle of his friendship without feeling the mastery of his personality. . . . To have met Whitman was a privilege, to have been his friend was an honor” (quoted in Green 137). Though Traubel seems to be suspicious of McKay—a feeling that eventuated in the publisher falling out with the literary executors around 1895—he was an ideal publisher for Whitman, allowing the printer-poet to direct more aspects of the production process than publishers would normally permit their authors. Whitman had a specific vision for his final miscellanies, and contemplated every detail of the binding, the illustrations, and the arrangement of the contents. Despite his illness and depression in 1891 and 1892, Whitman succeeded in this vision for Good-Bye My Fancy, his authorial project’s final phase.

div.head: Contemporary Reception of Good-Bye My Fancy
div.p: After Good-Bye My Fancy was published, bound, and distributed in May and June 1891, the project of the second miscellany—a venture that demanded from the poet’s scarce reserves of time, energy, and money—quickly receded into the past; he and his literary supporters turned their attention immediately onto what would become the deathbed edition of Leaves of Grass. What had been the topic for months in his international two-way correspondence and daily visits with Traubel is scarcely mentioned again. However, there is one important entry in the poet’s post-publication return to the book. When the August 1891 issue of Lippincott’s Magazine advertised the second annex, it announced “Walt Whitman’s Last” with a brief note written by the poet. “With Good-Bye My Fancy Walt Whitman has rounded out his life-work,” the editor, Joseph M. Stoddart, writes in a preface, noting that Whitman composed the note “only after considerable persuasion on the editor’s part.” Whitman’s note is a rambling three-paragraph summary of his poetics, beginning with Leaves of Grass. “Every page of my poetic or attempt at poetic utterance smacks of the living physical identity, date, environment, individuality, probably beyond anything known, and in a style often offensive to the conventions,” Whitman boasts. He then argues that Good-Bye My Fancy—“this new last cluster”—adheres to the same poetic theory, with the addition of one distinctive feature: “the clef is here changed to its lowest, and the little book is a lot of tremolos about old age, death, and faith.” Here, the poetry is without the melodic overtones one might associate with lilt and beauty in conventional poems, or indeed even in Whitman’s earlier work. Instead, he argues, “the physical just lingers, but almost vanishes” into a rumble on the lower register that, though perhaps unperceived in the earlier work, was always lending its undertones. While Whitman employs first-person pronouns throughout the piece, this usage recedes in the final paragraph, and by the final sentence he speaks of himself in third person: “The book is garrulous, irascible (like old Lear) and has various breaks and even tricks to avoid monotony. It will have to be ciphered and ciphered out long—and is probably in some respects the most curious part of its author’s baffling works.” Even this bit of advertising prose performs a dematerialization, a vanishing act of the poet’s famously large and multitudinous persona, in Ed Folsom’s words, “the material becoming more and more ‘unseen’” (“Whitman Getting Old” 243).

The distinction between dematerialization and material decay, however, is difficult to trace, especially through poetic imagery; reviewers were especially keen to note a tenor of when Good-Bye My Fancy was released in mid-1891. The New York Tribune’s anonymous review notes a “melancholy flavor about the whole of it, though the old man tries very hard to be cheerful,” and calls attention to the “grim frontispiece” that resembled “nothing so much as a death-mask”—an image taken from a May 1891 photograph by Thomas Eakins’s student Samuel Murray (prc.00086). For this reviewer, the book’s tone is too macabre to forgive its “so-called poetry” and “attempts at essay-writing.” And while the review recognizes Whitman’s book as his valediction volume, it also insightfully notes that Whitman “does not speculate much upon the future,” but instead is “chiefly interested in forecasting the ultimate destiny of Leaves of Grass.” As Whitman biographers have frequently noted, his last months were chiefly concerned with his legacy in print and the continued cultural presence of his poetic self. Though the Tribune reviewer doubts if much skill is evident in the contents in Whitman’s second miscellany, it is conceded that “the circumstances under which it was written impart a certain suggestion of pathos to it.”

Reviewers of Good-Bye My Fancy often referred to Whitman’s declining health, tying its appearance on the market to Whitman’s physical decline and inevitable disappearance. An anonymous review in The Independent—written with a tongue-in-cheek “sincere and sympathetic respect”—argues that the book is “evidently the work of a mind sorely diseased, worn out indeed,” and finds the prose selections “suggestive of unmitigated pathos.” The reviewer writes of their “curiosity tempered with sadness” from encountering Whitman’s “untold pangs of defeat,” and concludes that “there is nothing of any value whatever in this book. . . . So far as what purports to be literature is concerned, here is the end of a wasted life.” For these two negative reviewers, the failure of Good-Bye My Fancy was not primarily a question of craft, but of pathos; its contents were too tied to the emotional scene of Whitman’s physical decline to allow an honest review of the book.

More positive reviews were no less interested in this connection between the poet’s public aging and the release of Good-Bye My Fancy. Even a complimentary review—one that announces Good-Bye My Fancy as “the volume of the year, which should be especially precious to the American people”—enthusiastically identifies the poems as “these last few songs of [Whitman’s] old age.” This Poet Lore reviewer identified only as “C,” praises the “master’s touch,” and recognizes in the cadences echoes of Drum-Taps (1865), Whitman’s poetic documentation of the American Civil War. “We have space to quote only one,” the reviewer writes as introduction to quoting in full “Good-Bye My Fancy! / Farewell dear mate, dear love!,” a valedictory poem argued to “hold its own” with Tennyson’s “Crossing the Bar” (1889) and Robert Browning’s “Epilogue” from Asolando (1889).Whitman quotes the final stanzas of Tennyson’s “Crossing the Bar” in Good-Bye My Fancy as an example of the “poetic glints” able to “put the soul in rapport with death, or toward it.” Whitman himself makes the argument for his placement in the canon of recent valediction poetry by concluding the passage with his poem, “Now Finalè to the Shore” from Two Rivulets. As M. Wynn Thomas argues, “it might be worth considering the possibility that concealed in the two late annexes was Whitman’s obsessive conversation with Tennyson, ‘the boss of us all’ and the one great contemporary figure who contested with him the privilege of being the supreme poet of old age” (“Whitman, Tennyson” 177). The reviewer is aware of the controversial placement of Whitman’s Good-Bye My Fancy among those recent celebrated entries in the valediction genre from leading men of letters, noting that proper recognition of Whitman’s book would come only “when men have lost their rhythmical prejudices.” Surely, this review contends, there is room for Whitman in the canon of old poets saying their goodbyes.

Almost with a tone of amazement, an anonymous reviewer in The Literary Times declares, “Walt Whitman still lives,” characterizing him as “our old original individualistic American poet” and “the grand old fellow.” For this reviewer, Whitman’s age foregrounds the miscellany, “written as it were in defiance of augury.” The work is “in good fettle and equal to himself,” that is, equal to his reputation—the expected condition of his literary output. This pronouncedly old poet’s volume is “not the least interesting, especially his recollections of persons once famous, but long since gathered in by the reaper.” Whitman is depicted here as a grandfatherly poet, preserving the memories of the past and communicating them to his successors. For the reviewer, Whitman’s age and transgenerational memory reveal him to be an archetypal figure, since “indeed everything that Whitman has written is mystical, a shadowing forth of a half-comprehended entity in thought.” The brevity of the review does not allow its writer to press this argument that everything from the old poet has a mystical quality; had the review taken more space, it could have been worthwhile to see a mystical interpretation of Whitman’s depiction of his “palsied old shorn shell-fish condition.”

For a mystical consideration of age, one can turn to an unsigned review in the Critic, a journal that allowed ample space for the reviewer to more fully trace the themes of Good-Bye My Fancy. This allowance was perhaps due to the journal’s investment in the book’s contents, both prose and verse; “An Old Man’s Rejoinder,” “For Queen Victoria’s Birthday,” “Shakespeare in America,” “The Pallid Wreath,” and “Unassail’d Renown” had appeared in the Critic in 1890 and early 1891. The Critic’s reviewer argues that the theme of Good-Bye My Fancy is found in the poem, “L. of G.’s Purport”: “I sing of life, yet mind me well of death.”Incorrectly given as “mind me still of death” in the review. Though Whitman depicts his “shell-fish condition,” still, argues the reviewer, the shell “has a live soul in it capable still of radiant abalone-like iridescences.” The aspects of the book which were presented in The Literary Times as “mystical” and a “shadowing forth” stand out in the Critic as opalescence, the nacre of old age transitioning toward death:
Death, which inspires so many of these beautiful irregular lines, looms up magical and benign before a mind simply wondering, not abashed—the ‘eidόlon-yacht’ of his soul ready to put forth on its mirage-haunted seas with utmost trustfulness. Whitman’s beliefs come out singularly strong and triumphant here and there among the creed-leaves of the book: beliefs in future personality, identity, immortality, a merciful and loving God, progress, consciousness: he peoples that dim world with these, and it becomes immediately lustrous. . . . Indeed, the whole book is a book of ‘last words’ from dying lips sealing a life that has been blameless. There is no sound of lamentation or Job-cry in it, pervaded as it is with bright, broad optimism, the grace of benignant utterance, the egoism of a healthy and gracious child.
Contrary to the negative reviews in The Independent and The New York Tribune, the Critic reviewer does not find that Whitman’s preoccupation with his impending demise casts a dark morbidity over the work. Rather, death here is “magical and benign”; Whitman communicates his wonderment, trustfulness, and triumph, even a “bright, broad optimism.” The review opens with the Greek icon of the psychopomps, the likeness of Hermes escorting the soul into Hades, and suggests that Good-Bye My Fancy is Whitman’s psychopomps, “to convey his parting salutations to the afterworld.” This classical illustration presents Whitman’s afterlife as his readership, since the contemporary and subsequent audiences who pick up the book will give continued life to the valediction.

div.head: Good-Bye My Fancy Among the Disciples
div.p: As much as Whitman seems to have enjoyed discussing public reviews with Traubel, including those just cited, he was perhaps more interested in the private reviews from his supporters—the audience more immediately at-hand, and for whom he considered Good-Bye My Fancy a direct address. In late May, he sent off unbound copies to his closest supporters for their review. When Whitman revealed to Bucke his intention of publishing a second annex, the physician and confidant was incredulous: “this then I suppose is to be the end of the glorious Leaves? Well they are pretty complete—I hardly know what could be added with advantage” (loc.07126). Whitman sent him Good-Bye My Fancy’s poetry selection in March, which Bucke enthusiastically lauded as a “superb cluster.” He congratulated Whitman “upon having completed the greatest, most divine, most humanly helpful work that has ever so far proceeded from any individual man” (loc. 08130; loc. 08131, reprinted in WWC 8:119). On May 20, 1891, when Bucke received his unbound copy of the full text, he lost much of his original enthusiasm. It was a “most charming little vol.,” which “has not (of course) the power of the early books (either verse or prose) but has a charm of its own which will make it equal, in attractiveness, to any of your books” (loc.08144). After considering the book for three days, his opinion altered to one of gently mitigated support: “I like the little last leaves well—they are just what they should be under all the circumstances not great but very touching & charming” (loc.08145). Whitman’s response three days later defends Good-Bye My Fancy’s “off-handedness, even evidence of decrepitude” and “determin’d cartoon of Personality that dominates or rather stands behind all of L of G,” arguing for a formal or stylistic thread running throughout his published works (loc.08050). “Your own criticism of ‘Good-Bye’ is good,” replied Bucke’s next letter, “. . . its general ‘old age’ character is of course what it should have and if that involves (as in some sense it must) loss of power, dash and life it implies and gives something else just as good as these: undying courage, vim, and faith to the last in the scheme of the world and in man” (loc.08146). Whitman’s close friend concedes to the poet’s argument for the thread of continuity. After all, he was intimately familiar with the character of Whitman’s old age—his health issues and chronic depression—and could verify Good-Bye My Fancy’s portrayal of senescence, however much he might have preferred the middle-aged voice of the earlier poetry in Leaves of Grass.

Another of Whitman’s close associates, William Sloane Kennedy, received his advance copy of Good-Bye My Fancy on May 21, remarking in a postcard receipt of the book, “what pretty typography!” (loc.03164). “I enjoyed all,” he told Whitman, “think The Sunset Breeze the best of all.” Kennedy worked quickly to review the book, perhaps too quickly for Whitman, who wrote to Kennedy the following morning, “If you have not printed ab’t ‘Good–Bye’ keep it back for eight or ten days, as that w’d be preferable for reasons” (uva.00610). But Whitman was too late: his letter of May 22 arrived after Kennedy already printed a notice in the May 21 issue of the Boston Evening Transcript, having written and published the review on the same day he received the book (see also WWC 8:221). “Cutting open the leaves of advance sheets of another nosegay-bunch of prose and verse by Walt Whitman, we find many bits that will be relished by those who come to his pages for the first time,” he wrote. Again, he offers his opinion that “To the Sun-Set Breeze” is “by far the strongest poem in this good-by [sic] collection,” but notes that “old readers of Whitman will not find much up to the mark of old days.” Rather, Kennedy suggests the strength of the collection is its reliance on “touching memories,” making it an indispensable addition to Whitman’s corpus, and recalling the image of the grandfatherly figure communicating transgenerational knowledge.

In a letter of late March 1891, Whitman wrote to his English disciple Dr. John Johnston that he was hard at work on the proofs of Good-Bye My Fancy, but cautions: “don’t you look out for anything stirring—it is small any how” (loc.07905). Later, the Bolton disciples received their own unbound copy, sent to Johnston on May 17 (DBN 2:597). It arrived on the twenty-eighth, during what Johnston called a “fearfully busy week” (loc.02479). “As I was then overwhelmed with work I took the book at once to [fellow Bolton disciple James W. Wallace] & he has had it ever since until today,” Johnston wrote in receipt (loc.02479). “I could not let the mail go,” he adds, “without sending you my personal thanks for your generous gift which I shall prize very highly indeed & take time to absorb & assimilate.” Wallace wrote his own memo to Whitman, dated the evening he received the book from Johnston: “Johnston called on me just before I left the office tonight. . . . He had just received ‘Good-Bye My Fancy’& lent it to me that I might look it over tonight” (loc.04713). Since the Bolton group followed Whitman’s publications closely—with many of the pieces from magazines and newspapers mailed directly to them upon publication—Johnston prioritized reading “all the matter that I had not previously seen.” It was, evidently, a moving experience: “I will not attempt any description of my emotions & thoughts in doing so.—But it has been a sacred hour with me, full of deep, complex & tender feelings & thoughts.” Like Johnston, Wallace anticipated a more focused engagement with the text, “to absorb it as fully as may be.” The opportunity arose when, on June 18, he received his stitched copy sent personally from Whitman. “Of course I have seen Johnston’s copy of ‘Good Bye,’ but I only had it for one evening’s hasty reading. So that I am very glad to have a copy that I can read at leisure & absorb fully. And I am very proud to receive it from you, my dearest friend & benefactor,” he wrote (loc.04720). Contrary to the Tribune’s review, which argued the frontispiece resembled “nothing so much as a death-mask,” Wallace saw it depicting “a half-materialized spirit . . . grand & pensive, brooding over unfathomable mysteries, sad & tender,” thereby setting a mystical tone for the slim volume. The Bolton group was evidently pleased with Good-Bye My Fancy, since they ordered six additional bound copies from Whitman in June, and noted receiving them in July (loc.02485; loc.04724; see also WWC 8:270).

When examining significant opinions from Whitman’s disciples, it is important to include his most prolific devotee, Horace Traubel. In April 1891, Whitman wrote to Ellen O’Connor of his progress proofing Good-Bye My Fancy, admitting that he was “putting it through slowly” (nyp.00711). “Should not get along with it or anything without Horace Traubel,” he confesses, “comes every day, & is invaluable.” Whitman gave Traubel his unbound copy on April 29 and added a flyleaf with this personalized inscription: “Copy of / Good-Bye My Fancy / by Walt Whitman / April 1891 / Camden New Jersey / for Horace L Traubel” (WWC 8:172). As with November Boughs, Traubel was involved all along the way in the production of Good-Bye My Fancy, from concept to finished product. As before, Traubel acted as courier between Whitman, his printer, his bindery, and his proof-reader, carrying messages and corrected proofs; characteristically, he was also Whitman’s cheerleader, encouraging him to continue on the manuscript, and gently goading him when his focus was diverted from the project. “For the present, no doubt,” Traubel records Whitman telling him, “Good-Bye is our book—we must center on that” (WWC 8:176). Traubel’s notes even give the impression that he believed in the book when Whitman did not, notably during the periods of depression in late 1890 and early 1891. When Traubel tells Whitman “of the value I think belongs with ‘Good-Bye My Fancy’—that it has music and power,” Whitman is “incredulous” and responds with a barrage of questions “as to precise places and features” (WWC 8:43). Later, when Traubel shows his interest in an addition to the book, Whitman asks “But you really like it? . . . Does it seem actual?” (WWC 8:79). It seems as if Traubel could not convince the poet of the value in the work, and direct praise for Good-Bye My Fancy is muted throughout With Walt Whitman in Camden, reflecting perhaps the disciple’s own cooled enthusiasm.

div.head: Good-Bye My Fancy Today
div.p: When laying out the deathbed edition of Leaves of Grass in 1891, Whitman appended—“annexed,” as he would have it—the prose preface and the poems from Good-Bye My Fancy into the volume, flanked by the “Sands at Seventy” cluster of poems and the “A Backward Glance O’er Travel’d Roads ” essay from November Boughs. The material from the earlier miscellany first joined Leaves of Grass in late 1888 and early 1889, following the release of Complete Poems & Prose. On its title page, the deathbed edition calls special attention to its latest inclusions. Whitman’s authorial note on the copyright page calls “A Backward Glance”—placed at the end of the poetry like a period at the end of a sentence—“my concluding words,” and directs that, “as there are now several editions of L. of G., different texts and dates, I wish to say that I prefer and recommend this present one, complete, for future printing.” Editions in the century following have not been consistent in including the essay, and fair arguments for the freshness and originality of the earlier incarnations of Leaves of Grass—particularly the 1855 and 1860 editions, which have seen frequent reprinting and commentary—have questioned Whitman’s authorial preference for the 1891 edition. These earlier editions, grand as they are, are lacking the poems of life’s closing. In both the 1855 and 1860 editions, Whitman includes some formal parting from the reader, but these are the partings of middle age, and lack the vulnerability and insight into the final stage of life that make the poems in the final annexes so satisfying. In 1860’s “So Long,” for example, the poet declares that, “While my pleasure is yet at the full, I whisper So long.” He is able to depart because he has fully “announced the true theory of the youth, manhood, womanhood, of The States.” What is missing is the announcement of old age, when pleasure is far from full, conveyed in all its beautiful and troubling precarity in late-life poems like “To the Sun-Set Breeze” and “After the Supper and Talk.”

Thankfully, a growing number of scholars defend the poetry in the annexes in discussions of the evolution of Whitman’s style. Anton Vander Zee, Ed Folsom, and M. Wynn Thomas have argued for Whitman’s continued stylistic innovation; Thomas, for example, proposes that, while the younger Whitman “altered expression repeatedly, as epic, elegy, war poetry, love poetry, all assumed new forms in his work, . . . at life’s end, he succeeded in working one final miracle of transformation, producing a democratic poetry of old age” (179). Poets like Susan Howe, Robert Creeley, and Edward Hirsch have also turned to “Sands and Seventy” and “Good-Bye My fancy,” responding variously to Whitman’s “democratic poetry of old age.” However, these discussions rarely explore the interrelation between these final poems and the prose with which they were packaged in the final two miscellanies; it is more common to trace the afterlife of the poems from November Boughs and Good-Bye My Fancy than the prose, and though they are not among Whitman’s most frequently anthologized poems, they are certainly alluded to more than his prose from the same period. What would it mean to Whitman studies if his late-life poetry and prose were read in an integral relationship, as studies often interrelate the poetry of the 1855 Leaves of Grass and its prose preface or the documentary correlation between Drum-Taps and Memoranda During the War? It is in this regard that the Library of America’s Walt Whitman: Complete Poetry and Collected Prose (1982) has become a significant contribution, since it brings together the 1855 and 1891–1892 editions of Leaves of Grass and McKay’s Complete Prose Works, in which November Boughs and Good-Bye My Fancy appear as subheadings in the Table of Contents. In the Library of America edition, readers can piece together the final two miscellanies—the closest many will get since there has not been a reissue of either since the mid-1890s—thus the importance of these full reprintings on the Walt Whitman Archive.

“Things close down in age,” writes Robert Creeley, “like stores, like lights going off, like a world disappearing in a vacancy one had no thought might happen. . . . One sits and waits, most usually for the doctor.” There is, however, some compensation for this waiting: “one goes inside oneself, as it were, looks out from that ‘height’ with only imagination to give prospect.” Compiling Good-Bye My Fancy during his last year was therapeutic for the aged Whitman, a means of distraction from the chronic depression caused by his ailing body and vanishing relations. It also gave him a purpose, a drive toward some fulfillable goal that gave those months of solitude and infirmity some future-oriented direction. “I have observed that a life directed to an aim is in general better, richer, and healthier than an aimless one,” C. G. Jung argues, “and that it is better to go forwards with the stream of time than backwards against it” (792). Even when approaching the end of a lifetime, Jung suggests, setting goals is vital for a life worth living. In his two miscellanies, Whitman sets his sights on future readership—his legacy—and thereby transcends what he calls his “palsied old shorn and shellfish condition.” There is a deliberateness to the morbid tone criticized by reviewers, since through the individual pieces—and their aggregation—the poet confronts his inevitable death. The compiling, editing, and publishing of the miscellanies were lesser goals, the steps in the processing toward the major goal for Whitman to sort out, to classify and catalogue, his final theory of death. “As a doctor,” Jung continues, “I am convinced that it is hygienic—if I may use the word—to discover in death a goal towards which one can strive, and that shrinking away from it is something unhealthy and abnormal which robs the second half of life of its purpose.” Since middle age, Whitman’s journalism and poetry certainly included approaches to the end of life, but it is in these final works that readers encounter the culmination of his development—the final, fleeting blossom of the mortal selfhood celebrated in Leaves of Grass.
